name: itlib small and flat containers (itlib::flat_map, itlib::small_vector, itlib::static_vector)
workload: No benchmark exists for these containers; the only qualitative claim is in the header comment of flat_map.hpp and flat_set.hpp about smaller sets of elements versus std::map/std::set.
claimed_speedup: No numbers. Header comment in include/itlib/flat_map.hpp: "It generally performs much faster than std::map for smaller sets of elements" (same sentence for std::set in flat_set.hpp). small_vector.hpp and static_vector.hpp only claim cache-local data; README calls them "similar to boost::small_vector / boost::static_vector / boost::flat_map" with no speed statement.
stars_or_usage: 212 stars; a search snippet (not opened) says VTK/diy2 merge requests replace chobo small_vector with itlib small_vector
tradeoffs: Single-header, MIT, C++11. flat_map/flat_set keep a sorted std::vector-compatible container (swappable via template argument, so itlib::static_vector or small_vector can back them); lookup O(log n), insert and erase O(n); iterators and references invalidated on insert/erase; template signature differs from std::map (last parameter is a container, not an allocator). small_vector has a static buffer then falls back to heap; static_vector has fixed capacity.
caveats: No numeric comparison against std::map, std::vector, boost::container::flat_map or boost::container::small_vector anywhere found: repo has no bench folder, test/ holds one benchmark (b-rand_dist.cpp, picobench, random distributions only, no results published), issues search returned nothing on performance (7 issues), the original Chobolabs/chobo-shl README has only the same "better cache locality" wording, and a web search found no third-party numbers. Tier D under the seed-pass rule; 212 stars is below the usual notability bar for D entries, so the orchestrator may drop it. Header says only "generally ... for smaller sets", no sizes or machine.

name: Coost fastring and fastream
workload: No benchmark published for fastring (string) or fastream (append-only char stream, alternative to std::ostringstream/snprintf).
claimed_speedup: No numbers. The v3.0.1 and v3.0.2 README feature lists only say "Efficient stream (fastream)" and "Efficient string (fastring)"; neither README, headers (include/co/fastring.h, fastream.h at v3.0.2) nor the benchmark folder carry a measurement.
tradeoffs: fastring is not a drop-in std::string: it derives from a fast::stream byte buffer and relies on coost's own memory allocator; coost issue #282 (2022) notes there is no small string optimization, so small strings may be slower than std::string with the default allocator; the maintainer said SSO may be considered later and the issue was closed in May 2025 without numbers. Pulls in the rest of the coost library headers.
caveats: Tier D, no numbers anywhere found. On master (tag v4.0.0 of 2026-09-15 and v4.0.1 of 2026-09-28) include/co/fastring.h and fastream.h no longer exist (raw fetch returns 404); they exist at v3.0.2. master has co::string in include/co/string.h and benchmark/string.cc comparing std::string with co::string (assign, find) but no published results, so the fastring/fastream lead is now obsolete in current code. The project docs site (idealvin.github.io) could not be reached from this environment, so any numbers only there were not seen.
found_via: seed-record pass: https://github.com/idealvin/coost (README at master and v3.0.2, benchmark/ folder, include/co listing, issue #282); two web searches for fastring/fastream benchmarks found nothing

name: Coost co/json
workload: Parse and stringify of minified twitter.json (simdjson's jsonexamples/twitter.json), average microseconds per operation, co/json DOM versus RapidJSON Document/Writer.
claimed_speedup: README table (us, co/json vs rapidjson): win stringify 569 vs 2089 (3.6x), parse 924 vs 2495 (2.7x); mac stringify 783 vs 1289 (1.6x), parse 1097 vs 1658 (1.5x); linux stringify 468 vs 1359 (2.9x), parse 764 vs 1070 (1.4x). The benchmark branch also compares simdjson (linux, us): parse 666.979 co/json vs 1233.701 rapidjson vs 385.3 simdjson; stringify 1660 co/json vs 2503 rapidjson vs 1779 simdjson; minimal input parse 457.381 / 1057.799 / 351.752, stringify 981 / 2243 / 2298.
compiler_and_flags: Benchmark branch xmake.lua uses set_optimize("fastest"); compiler, version and exact flags not stated; RAPIDJSON_SSE42 defined only if CO_SSE42 is set.
hardware: Not stated: only OS labels win, mac, linux (the log benchmark text in the same branch says its Linux numbers came from the Windows Subsystem for Linux); no CPU model.
tradeoffs: Part of the coost library (co::Json/json::any, fluent API, own allocator and fastring/co::string types), not a standalone single header; DOM only. Benchmark code is public (benchmark branch: benchmark/json_bm.cc, rapidjson.h, simdjson folder, xmake.lua) but is not on master.
caveats: First-party, partial methodology, so tier C. Table is identical to the v3.0.2 README, so it predates coost 4.0 (2026-09-15) whose API changed (json::any, co::string); master test/jbm.cc now times only co/json, and the RapidJSON/simdjson comparison code is only on the old benchmark branch (co::Json, fastring). The README calls the figures averages, but in json_bm.cc the stringify figure is a single timed call after one warm-up, parse is the mean of 1000 loops. RapidJSON baseline is default Document::Parse with default flags (no in-situ, no SIMD unless CO_SSE42) and its stringify includes building a StringBuffer and copying into std::string. README and benchmark-branch readme give different numbers for the same rows (branch: linux parse 1005 vs 1270 us, stringify 920 vs 2106 us), and the branch's own simdjson comparison shows simdjson parsing faster than co/json on Linux (385.3 vs 666.979 us). No CPU, compiler or RAM stated.

name: sfl-library small and static containers (sfl::small_vector, sfl::static_vector, sfl::small_flat_map)
workload: No published measurement for small_vector, static_vector or small_flat_map; the repo's benchmark/ folder holds benchmark sources for other components only.
claimed_speedup: No numbers. README and doc pages describe small_vector as a vector that "embeds small statically allocated storage internally to avoid dynamic memory allocation" and static_vector as backed entirely by static storage "cache-friendly"; the only comparative wording is qualitative (devector "faster insertion and deletion at the front" than vector; segmented_devector "a superior alternative to std::deque").
compiler_and_flags: Benchmark makefile (not tied to published results): g++ -std=c++20 -O3 -DNDEBUG
tradeoffs: Header-only C++11; small_vector keeps N elements inline then falls back to heap; static_vector never allocates and exceeding N is undefined behavior; containers support stateful and fancy-pointer allocators and many are constexpr in C++20. Interface follows std::vector, not a boost::container::small_vector drop-in.
caveats: Tier D under the seed-pass rule: no numeric comparison found. benchmark/src has unordered_map.cpp (sfl vs std::unordered_map vs boost::unordered_map, random insert/lookup/erase/copy), small_unordered_map.cpp and segmented_devector.cpp (vs std::deque and boost::container::deque, 10M integers, median of 20 runs), but none cover small_vector, static_vector or small_flat_map and no results are published in the repo (commit 'Reworked benchmarks' 2026-03-10). boost::container::small_vector and absl::InlinedVector are not benchmarked at all. 164 stars is below the usual notability bar for tier D, so the orchestrator may drop it; if the benchmark results get published, unordered_map or segmented_devector would be the better-documented components.
